title: 5. Fit mixed models
5. Fit mixed models
Longitudinal data and mixed models
text: This page explains the model behind the repeated-measures outcomes (ACT, AQLQ, PACQLQ, AFS and self-reported adherence) in general terms. It says nothing about this trial’s results. The last methods page shows where each idea appears in the code.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Why repeated measures need their own model
text:
Why repeated measures need their own model
In a trial with visits at baseline and at several follow-up times, each participant contributes several measurements. Measurements from the same person are more alike than measurements from different people: someone with well-controlled asthma at baseline tends to stay better controlled than average. Treating all rows as independent ignores that relationship and can give incorrect uncertainty estimates; the direction of the error depends on the comparison.
A linear mixed model represents this with a participant-specific shift in the expected score, a random intercept. The fixed effects describe the average course of each arm over time, and the random intercept absorbs each person’s persistent difference from that average. This is the model fitted with lme4 (Bates et al. 2015):


Click to show/hide R Code
# Each participant (study_id_screening) gets a random intercept
lmer(act_score ~ time_factor * studyarm + (1 | study_id_screening), data = visits)


In this model, a random intercept together with constant residual variance assumes equal residual correlation between any two visits from the same person, however far apart they are. Richer structures (random slopes for time, or a correlation that falls off with distance) are possible, at the cost of more parameters.
Read the formula as “model asthma-control score using visit, arm and how their relationship changes, while allowing participants to have different starting levels.”







R notation
How to read it




outcome ~ predictors
The outcome on the left is modeled using the terms on the right


time_factor * studyarm
Include visit, arm and the visit-by-arm interaction


(1 \| study_id_screening)
Allow a participant-specific intercept


data = visits
Find the named columns in this dataset



An interaction allows the arm difference to vary with visit. A factor tells R that values are categories. The reference category is the starting point against which the other categories are expressed.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Time as a factor, not a line
text:
Time as a factor, not a line
time_factor treats each visit (0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12 months) as its own category, so the model estimates a separate mean for each arm at each visit without assuming a straight line or any other shape over time. With six visits that’s 12 means (6 visits × 2 arms). The price is more parameters than a linear trend; the gain is that a rise and then a fall, or an early change that levels off, are described as they are.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
text:
What the coefficients mean
With R’s default coding, control is the reference arm and baseline is the reference visit. The model time_factor * studyarm then has these fixed effects:







Coefficient
Meaning




(Intercept)
Mean in the control arm at baseline


studyarm1
Difference between arms at baseline


time_factor2, time_factor4, …
Change from baseline in the control arm at each visit


time_factor2:studyarm1, …
How much more (or less) the intervention arm changed from baseline than the control arm, at each visit



The last row matters most. Each visit-by-arm term is a difference in change from baseline: the arm difference at that visit minus the arm difference at baseline. This is what the plots mean by “adjusted for baseline differences”. This subtraction defines a change contrast; it does not guarantee that baseline imbalance or regression to the mean has been accounted for appropriately. It is different from using the baseline score as a covariate in an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) (Vickers and Altman 2001).
The arm difference at a given visit itself, with no baseline subtraction, is not one coefficient: it’s studyarm1 plus that visit’s interaction term. Adding a subgroup to this model is covered in Interactions. Getting such combinations, with their confidence intervals, is the subject of Effects behind an interaction.

A small invented example
These means are entirely invented, not trial results.



Arm
Baseline score
Follow-up score
Change




Control
10
12
+2


Intervention
11
15
+4



The follow-up arm difference is 15 − 12 = 3 points. The difference in change is 4 − 2 = 2 points, equivalently the follow-up difference of 3 minus the baseline difference of 1. Both describe these numbers, but they answer different questions. Whether a score difference is clinically important requires the instrument’s interpretation, not just a p-value.
For a short explanation of baseline adjustment, see Vickers and Altman’s Statistics Note (Vickers and Altman 2001).

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Missed visits and missing at random
text:
Missed visits and missing at random
A participant who misses a visit can still contribute their other observed measurements to a mixed model. This does not require filling in a score for the missed visit. Observations with missing model predictors, such as a subgroup classification, are a separate problem.
Missing at random (MAR) means that, after accounting for relevant information already recorded—such as treatment group and earlier asthma scores—whether someone misses a visit does not additionally depend on the asthma score we would have measured at that visit. “At random” does not mean that visits were missed without a reason (Sterne et al. 2009).
For example, missed visits related to previously recorded poor asthma control can be compatible with MAR. Missed visits related to unrecorded worsening symptoms may violate it, if that relationship remains after accounting for the observed information. These are hypothetical examples, not explanations established for this trial.
Likelihood-based mixed models can support valid inference under MAR when the outcome model is correctly specified and represents the relevant observed information. Choosing a mixed model does not establish MAR, and observed data alone cannot distinguish MAR from missingness that still depends on unobserved outcomes (Sterne et al. 2009).

What multiple imputation adds
Multiple imputation creates several plausible versions of the missing values, analyzes each completed dataset, and pools the estimates while accounting for uncertainty about the missing values. It does not recover the actual missed measurements (Sterne et al. 2009).
It is not automatically necessary just because outcome visits were missed: the mixed model already uses incomplete outcome trajectories under MAR. Imputation may add value when model predictors are missing or when other recorded variables help predict missingness and missing outcomes. For longitudinal analyses, the imputation model must respect repeated observations within participants and the interactions used in the analysis.
Ordinary MAR-based imputation does not solve missingness that depends on unobserved outcomes. Sensitivity analyses instead examine how conclusions change under explicitly different assumptions. Whether to add imputation or such analyses here remains a scientific decision; this explanation does not change the analysis.
For an accessible introduction, see Box 1 and the practical discussion in Sterne and colleagues’ BMJ article (Sterne et al. 2009).

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Other models for the same question
text:
Other models for the same question
The random-intercept mixed model is one of several reasonable ways to analyse repeated measures in a trial. Two common alternatives are worth knowing, because readers will meet them in other trials and because each makes a different trade-off. This trial uses neither; the comparison is here to explain the choice.










Linear mixed model (used here)
Mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM)
Generalized estimating equations (GEE)




How it handles a person’s repeated visits
A random intercept per participant
No random effects; models the correlation between visits directly
No random effects; a “working” guess at the correlation


Correlation between visits
Implied: the same for any two visits
Estimated freely for every pair of visits (unstructured)
Treated as a nuisance; the standard errors are robust to a wrong guess


How it is fitted
Likelihood
Likelihood
Estimating equations, with no full distributional assumption


Missed visits
Valid if missing at random (see above)
Valid if missing at random
Valid only if missing completely at random, unless weighted


Main cost
The equal-correlation assumption
Many correlation parameters: 21 for six visits
Weaker missing-data protection; robust standard errors are too small in small samples



MMRM is the most common primary analysis for continuous outcomes in regulatory trials with fixed visits (Mallinckrodt et al. 2008). Its unstructured correlation avoids assuming that a person’s visits two months apart are as alike as visits a year apart. The price is many parameters, which a small pilot may not support, especially within subgroups. In its usual form an MMRM also treats the baseline score as a covariate rather than as one of the outcomes, which changes the estimate from a difference in change from baseline to a baseline-adjusted difference at each visit (Coffman et al. 2016). That is a different question, not just a different method.
GEE describe the average outcome in each group without modelling individuals (Liang and Zeger 1986). Their robust standard errors stay valid even if the assumed correlation is wrong. But in their basic form they assume that missed visits are unrelated to anything measured, which is a stronger assumption than missing at random; weighting by the probability of attending each visit relaxes it (Robins et al. 1995). With few participants, robust standard errors are biased downwards and need a small-sample correction (Mancl and DeRouen 2001).
For a continuous outcome, all three can estimate the same treatment effect, and the same tools turn the fit into estimates and figures. This pilot uses the random-intercept model because it uses every observed visit under missing at random with few parameters.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
text:
Count outcomes are different
The 12-month health care use counts and the rescue inhaler counts are one value per participant, not repeated measures, so they don’t need a mixed model. They are fitted with negative binomial regression on the log scale, with the log of each person’s follow-up time as an offset, so the model describes rates (events per day of follow-up) rather than raw counts. On the log scale, exponentiated coefficients are incidence rate ratios: an arm effect of 0.8 means the intervention arm’s rate is 80% of the control arm’s.

Counts, rates and the offset
In an invented example, 6 events over 60 days and 3 events over 30 days have the same rate: 0.1 events per day. Comparing the counts alone would miss that equality. The offset supplies the exposure duration with its coefficient fixed, so the model compares rates. Negative binomial regression additionally allows counts to vary more than a Poisson model assumes. Neither choice repairs incorrectly defined event counts or follow-up windows.
An IRR of 1 means equal modeled rates; an IRR below 1 means a lower rate in the intervention arm, with the direction reversed above 1. A 95% confidence interval crossing 1 includes equal rates among the values compatible with the data and model at that confidence level; it does not prove equivalence.
For technical depth after the examples, Bates and colleagues explain the mixed-model implementation (Bates et al. 2015). The MASS reference documents the negative binomial function (MASS authors, n.d.).

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text: Clean the app-recorded inhaler data, count rescue use, compute controller proportion of days covered (PDC), and build the participant-level data for the count models.

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Clean medication records
Start with individual app records. Rows without an identifier are removed, and medication names help classify records whose app label is not already Control or Rescue. Joining study_dates adds each participant’s follow-up boundaries. The current filter applies the upper boundary at the 12-month visit; the missing lower boundary at consent is tracked in #3. Classification and time-window checks determine which records contribute to every later summary.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Records with no study ID are not participants and are excluded from all
# analyses (study team decision). Records are relabelled controller or rescue
# by medication name where the app's own label is not Control or Rescue.
medication_data_clean <- raw_medications %>%
  filter(!is.na(SUBJECTID)) %>%
  mutate(med_type_clean = case_when(
    Med.Type == "Control" ~ "Control",
    Med.Type == "Rescue" ~ "Rescue",
    str_detect(Medication, paste(controller_medication_names, collapse = "|")) ~
      "Control",
    str_detect(Medication, paste(rescue_medication_names, collapse = "|")) ~
      "Rescue"
  )) %>%
  left_join(study_dates, by = c("SUBJECTID" = "study_id_screening")) %>%
  # Drop records after the 12-month visit. See issue #3 for the lower bound.
  filter(PuffDate <= follow_up_12_month)

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Count rescue use
group_by(SUBJECTID) followed by summarize() reduces many records to one row per participant. Here n() counts records (the code calls these rescue puffs), while n_distinct(PuffDate) counts distinct recorded date values. The latter represents days only if the field has been reduced to calendar dates; timestamps within the same day would remain distinct. The second calculation restricts records to the per-protocol cutoff before joining the summaries.


Click to show/hide R Code
rescue_medication <- medication_data_clean %>%
  filter(med_type_clean == "Rescue") %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod, Medication, PuffDate, `Puff(EST)`)

# One row per participant: rescue puffs and rescue days, ITT
total_rescue_medication_uses <- rescue_medication %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID) %>%
  summarize(
    rescue_puffs_itt = n(),
    rescue_days_itt = n_distinct(PuffDate)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, rescue_puffs_itt, rescue_days_itt)

# Add the per-protocol counts (records on or before the glitch date)
total_rescue_medication_uses <- rescue_medication %>%
  filter(PuffDate <= glitch_date) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID) %>%
  summarize(
    rescue_puffs_pp = n(),
    rescue_days_pp = n_distinct(PuffDate)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, rescue_puffs_pp, rescue_days_pp) %>%
  right_join(total_rescue_medication_uses)

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Count controller use
Controller records are grouped by participant, study-day offset and recorded date. The code counts rows and distinct Puff(EST) values, then keeps distinct summary rows. These summaries describe recorded use. Their correspondence to actual doses depends on the export’s definition of a record and its date fields.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Controller puffs and uses per participant per day
control_medication <- medication_data_clean %>%
  filter(med_type_clean == "Control") %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod, Medication, PuffDate, `Puff(EST)`) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod, PuffDate) %>%
  mutate(control_puffs = n()) %>%
  mutate(control_uses = n_distinct(`Puff(EST)`)) %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod, control_puffs, control_uses, PuffDate) %>%
  distinct()

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Controller day grid
A proportion needs days with no recorded use in its denominator too. The grid supplies candidate participant-days, then the join attaches controller records; unmatched grid rows receive zero recorded puffs.
Read the implementation carefully: its candidate days come from unique(medication_data_clean$StudyPeriod), not an independently generated sequence of every calendar day. Its identifiers also come from a numeric sequence (#15). If an eligible study-day offset never appears in the medication data, it cannot enter this grid. This is a denominator issue, not evidence that those days had no use.
The quarter label means a visit interval here; the intervals are not all three months long. The interval’s value is attached to the visit that ends it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Every participant-day from consent to the 12-month visit, with the visit
# interval it falls in. See issues #4 and #15.
full_date_grid <- expand.grid(
  seq(1, n_subject_ids, 1),
  unique(medication_data_clean$StudyPeriod)
) %>%
  rename(SUBJECTID = Var1, StudyPeriod = Var2) %>%
  left_join(study_dates, by = c("SUBJECTID" = "study_id_screening")) %>%
  arrange(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod) %>%
  mutate(consent_date = as.Date(consent_date)) %>%
  mutate(PuffDate = consent_date + StudyPeriod) %>%
  filter(PuffDate <= follow_up_12_month) %>%
  mutate(quarter = case_when(
    (PuffDate >= consent_date) & (PuffDate < follow_up_2_months) ~
      "0-2 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_2_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_4_months) ~
      "2-4 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_4_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_6_months) ~
      "4-6 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_6_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_9_months) ~
      "6-9 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_9_months) & (PuffDate <= follow_up_12_month) ~
      "9-12 months"
  )) %>%
  # Interval controller PDC is attached to the visit that closes the interval
  mutate(time_factor = case_when(
    (PuffDate >= consent_date) & (PuffDate < follow_up_2_months) ~ "2",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_2_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_4_months) ~ "4",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_4_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_6_months) ~ "6",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_6_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_9_months) ~ "9",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_9_months) & (PuffDate <= follow_up_12_month) ~ "12"
  )) %>%
  mutate(time_factor = as.factor(time_factor)) %>%
  select(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod, PuffDate, quarter, time_factor)

# Days with no controller record get zero puffs and uses
control_medication <- right_join(control_medication, full_date_grid) %>%
  mutate(control_puffs = ifelse(is.na(control_puffs), 0, control_puffs)) %>%
  mutate(control_uses = ifelse(is.na(control_uses), 0, control_uses)) %>%
  arrange(SUBJECTID, StudyPeriod)

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Controller PDC
Proportion of days covered (PDC) is the name used here for the fraction of represented days with at least one recorded controller puff. It is not a pharmacy-refill measure. day_is_covered is 1 for such a day and 0 otherwise, so its mean is the fraction covered. In a wholly invented example, four covered days among ten eligible days gives 0.40 (40%). Four covered days in a grid containing only eight of those days gives 0.50: the denominator matters.
The code calculates an overall value and a value for each visit interval, both with and without the cutoff. Zero recorded use is a coding assumption about the app record, not proof that a person took no medication. Read this alongside the preceding grid section.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Proportion of days with at least one controller puff, for the year
controller_pdc <- control_medication %>%
  mutate(day_is_covered = ifelse(control_puffs > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID) %>%
  summarize(controller_pdc_itt = mean(day_is_covered)) %>%
  ungroup()

controller_pdc <- control_medication %>%
  mutate(day_is_covered = ifelse(control_puffs > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  filter(PuffDate <= glitch_date) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID) %>%
  summarize(controller_pdc_pp = mean(day_is_covered)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(controller_pdc)

# The same, within each visit interval
controller_pdc_quarter <- control_medication %>%
  mutate(day_is_covered = ifelse(control_puffs > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID, time_factor) %>%
  summarize(controller_pdc_quarter_itt = mean(day_is_covered)) %>%
  rename(study_id_screening = SUBJECTID) %>%
  ungroup()

controller_pdc_quarter <- control_medication %>%
  mutate(day_is_covered = ifelse(control_puffs > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  filter(PuffDate <= glitch_date) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID, time_factor) %>%
  summarize(controller_pdc_quarter_pp = mean(day_is_covered)) %>%
  rename(study_id_screening = SUBJECTID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(controller_pdc_quarter)

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Baseline count data
This returns to one row per participant using the baseline REDCap records, where the code retrieves the health-care-use count fields. Missing counts are changed to zero before 999 codes are changed to missing. Those operations have different meanings: zero asserts no events, while missing means the count is unknown. The analysis plan leaves this handling open.
Follow-up is expressed in days for use in count-model offsets. The current per-protocol calculation uses min() across participants rather than a separate minimum for each participant (#2); it is not used by the displayed count models.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per participant: baseline values and 12-month health care use
baseline_clean_data <- clean_asthma_data_itt %>%
  filter(time_linear == 0) %>%
  # A missing count is set to 0
  mutate(across(
    .cols = all_of(hospital_count_outcomes),
    .fns = ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), 0, .x)
  )) %>%
  # A count of 999 is set to missing
  mutate(across(
    .cols = all_of(hospital_count_outcomes),
    .fns = ~ ifelse(.x == 999, NA, .x)
  )) %>%
  mutate(followup_time_itt = as.numeric(
    difftime(follow_up_12_month, consent_date, units = "days")
  )) %>%
  # See issue #2: min() returns one value for everyone
  mutate(followup_time_pp = min(
    as.numeric(difftime(follow_up_12_month, consent_date, units = "days")),
    as.numeric(difftime(glitch_date, consent_date, units = "days"))
  ))

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Merge medication summaries
The participant-level rescue and controller summaries are attached to baseline data for count models. Participants without a matching rescue summary are assigned zero recorded rescue use. Controller PDC is joined separately, and interval PDC is added to the visit datasets. Each join needs a unique matching summary per intended key: participant for annual summaries, participant and visit for interval summaries. The joins chapter explains why key uniqueness matters (Wickham et al. 2023).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Participants with no rescue records have zero rescue use
rescue_medication_merged <- left_join(
  baseline_clean_data,
  total_rescue_medication_uses,
  by = c("study_id_screening" = "SUBJECTID")
) %>%
  mutate(rescue_puffs_itt = ifelse(
    is.na(rescue_puffs_itt), 0, rescue_puffs_itt
  )) %>%
  mutate(rescue_days_itt = ifelse(
    is.na(rescue_days_itt), 0, rescue_days_itt
  )) %>%
  mutate(rescue_puffs_pp = ifelse(
    is.na(rescue_puffs_pp), 0, rescue_puffs_pp
  )) %>%
  mutate(rescue_days_pp = ifelse(
    is.na(rescue_days_pp), 0, rescue_days_pp
  ))

controller_medication_merged <- left_join(
  baseline_clean_data,
  controller_pdc,
  by = c("study_id_screening" = "SUBJECTID")
)

# Interval controller PDC joined to the visit data
clean_asthma_data_itt <- clean_asthma_data_itt %>%
  left_join(controller_pdc_quarter) %>%
  select(-controller_pdc_quarter_pp)

clean_asthma_data_pp <- clean_asthma_data_pp %>%
  left_join(controller_pdc_quarter) %>%
  select(-controller_pdc_quarter_itt)

title: 3. Derive medication outcomes
text:
Medication by interval
This further summary groups records by participant, visit interval and medication type. complete() adds missing combinations of the values present in the data; it does not discover participants or intervals absent from those values. Added count cells become zero. The final interval here excludes the 12-month endpoint, whereas the day-grid calculation includes it; #4 tracks that mismatch.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Puff and day counts by visit interval and inhaler type. See issue #4.
medication_data_quarter <- medication_data_clean %>%
  mutate(quarter = case_when(
    (PuffDate >= consent_date) & (PuffDate < follow_up_2_months) ~
      "0-2 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_2_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_4_months) ~
      "2-4 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_4_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_6_months) ~
      "4-6 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_6_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_9_months) ~
      "6-9 months",
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_9_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_12_month) ~
      "9-12 months"
  )) %>%
  mutate(quarter_number_days = case_when(
    (PuffDate >= consent_date) & (PuffDate < follow_up_2_months) ~
      difftime(follow_up_2_months, consent_date, units = "days"),
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_2_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_4_months) ~
      difftime(follow_up_4_months, follow_up_2_months, units = "days"),
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_4_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_6_months) ~
      difftime(follow_up_6_months, follow_up_4_months, units = "days"),
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_6_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_9_months) ~
      difftime(follow_up_9_months, follow_up_6_months, units = "days"),
    (PuffDate >= follow_up_9_months) & (PuffDate < follow_up_12_month) ~
      difftime(follow_up_12_month, follow_up_9_months, units = "days"),
  ))

medication_quarter_counts <- medication_data_quarter %>%
  filter(!is.na(quarter)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(med_type_clean)) %>%
  group_by(SUBJECTID, quarter, med_type_clean) %>%
  mutate(number_puffs = n()) %>%
  mutate(number_days = n_distinct(PuffDate)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(
    SUBJECTID, quarter, quarter_number_days, med_type_clean,
    number_puffs, number_days
  ) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  complete(SUBJECTID, quarter, med_type_clean) %>%
  mutate(number_puffs = ifelse(is.na(number_puffs), 0, number_puffs)) %>%
  mutate(number_days = ifelse(is.na(number_days), 0, number_days))

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text: This page explains what the p-value of an interaction term tests, and what it doesn’t. It uses no results from this trial.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: It tests a difference between effects
text:
It tests a difference between effects
The p-value of an arm × subgroup interaction tests one null hypothesis: the arm effect is the same in every level of the subgroup. A small p-value is evidence that the effects differ. It is not a test of whether the intervention works in any one subgroup.
A p-value measures how incompatible the observed test statistic is with a specified null hypothesis and model assumptions. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that a result happened “by chance.” Here the null is about equal effects on the scale being tested.
Altman and Bland make the general point: to compare two estimates, test their difference directly; don’t compare their separate p-values (Altman and Bland 2003).
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: “Significant in one subgroup and not the other” is not evidence of a difference
text:
“Significant in one subgroup and not the other” is not evidence of a difference
A common mistake is to fit the model in each subgroup separately, find p < 0.05 in one and p > 0.05 in the other, and conclude the intervention works only in the first. Two estimates can be almost identical while one crosses 0.05 and the other doesn’t, especially when the subgroups differ in size. Brookes and colleagues showed by simulation how often subgroup-specific tests produce this pattern when the true effect is the same in both groups, and that the interaction test is the right comparison (Brookes et al. 2004).
For example, two wholly invented estimates could both be an IRR of 0.80, with intervals of 0.65–0.98 and 0.55–1.16. One interval excludes 1 and the other includes it, yet the estimated effects are identical. The interaction test directly addresses whether the effects differ.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
It has low power
Power is the probability that a study’s test detects a specified effect when that effect is present, under the assumptions used for the calculation. A trial sized to detect the overall effect has far less power to detect an interaction of the same size. In Brookes and colleagues’ simulations, a trial with 80% power for the overall effect had only about 29% power for an interaction of that magnitude, and roughly four times the sample size was needed to match (Brookes et al. 2004). In a pilot trial this matters even more: a large p-value for interaction is weak evidence that the effects are the same.

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
It depends on the scale
As the Interactions page explains, an interaction is measured on a scale. A test on the ratio scale (count models) and a test on the difference scale (mixed models) are answering different questions, and can disagree on the same data.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
Many tests
Each subgroup variable, outcome, population and visit adds tests. With several subgroups, several outcomes, two populations and an interaction p-value at every visit, some small p-values are expected by chance alone. Wang and colleagues’ guidance on reporting subgroup analyses asks that the number of subgroup analyses be stated, that prespecified and post hoc analyses be distinguished, and that interaction tests rather than subgroup-specific tests be the basis for claims of different effects (Wang et al. 2007). The retrospective analysis plan currently treats the subgroup analyses as post hoc unless protocol documentation establishes otherwise; the code applies no multiplicity adjustment.

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: Report the effects, not only the p-value
text:
Report the effects, not only the p-value
Because the interaction p-value says nothing about the size of the effect in each group, it’s best reported alongside the effect within each subgroup level, with its confidence interval (Knol and VanderWeele 2012). Effects behind an interaction shows how to get those.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
Reading a subgroup result
Read the estimated effects and intervals first, then the interaction p-value. Ask what scale was tested, how precise each estimate is, and how many subgroup comparisons were examined. A wide interval and a large interaction p-value can leave substantial differences unresolved.
Start with Altman and Bland’s short Statistics Note (Altman and Bland 2003). Wang and colleagues provide a clinical-trial reporting checklist (Wang et al. 2007); Brookes and colleagues give the simulation evidence on power (Brookes et al. 2004).

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
The clinical question is usually “How large is the intervention effect in each subgroup, and how uncertain is it?” A model’s printed coefficient table may not answer that directly. A contrast is a requested comparison of model estimates, such as intervention minus control within a subgroup.
In the invented interaction example, the subgroup IRRs were 0.80 and 1.00. Those are the effects to report, with intervals, alongside the test comparing them. You do not need to calculate a covariance matrix by hand to extract them.
The code below is illustrative, displayed without execution, and assumes models have already been fitted with the variables shown. It does not run in this site’s build or add emmeans to the analysis pipeline. The intended ordering is control then intervention, and baseline then follow-up visits; changing the factor order can reverse a comparison.

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
With emmeans
emmeans computes these combinations from the fitted model, without refitting and without writing out terms by hand (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026). For the count model:


Click to show/hide R Code
library(emmeans)

emmeans(fit, ~ studyarm | prefer_language, type = "response") %>%
  contrast("revpairwise") %>%
  confint()


This gives one row per language: the intervention-vs-control IRR (a ratio column) with its confidence interval. On the log scale, comparisons are differences of logs, which become ratios when back-transformed. Both arms are compared at the same follow-up time, so the offset cancels out of the ratio.
For the mixed model, the arm difference at each visit within each subgroup level:


Click to show/hide R Code
emmeans(fit_lmer, ~ studyarm | time_factor * prefer_language) %>%
  contrast("revpairwise") %>%
  confint()


These are differences on the score scale, with no baseline subtraction. To get the change-from-baseline differences that the model’s interaction terms describe, ask for an interaction contrast between arms and between each visit and baseline:


Click to show/hide R Code
emmeans(fit_lmer, ~ studyarm * time_factor | prefer_language) %>%
  contrast(interaction = c("revpairwise", "trt.vs.ctrl")) %>%
  confint()


For lmer models, emmeans chooses its own degrees-of-freedom method (Kenward–Roger or Satterthwaite; see its documentation), so p-values can differ slightly from the ones lmerTest reports.
Read ~ studyarm | prefer_language as “compare arms separately within each language.” Here the vertical bar groups requested comparisons; it is not the random-intercept notation in an lmer() formula. revpairwise reverses the usual pairwise direction so the stated factor order gives intervention versus control. confint() explicitly requests confidence intervals. Check the printed contrast labels before interpreting the signs or ratios.
For a count outcome, a wholly invented output of ratio 0.80 with interval 0.60–1.07 would indicate an estimated 20% lower rate, with uncertainty extending from a lower rate to a slightly higher rate. For a score outcome, a difference of 2 points is measured in that score’s units. An interval for a mean or contrast is not the range of scores expected for individual participants.
Start with the package’s quick-start guide. The interval and summary reference explains confint(), scales and inference options (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026). These examples were checked against the published 2.0.5 documentation; they still need execution on synthetic data in this project.

title: Effects behind an interaction
section: By refitting with a different reference level
text:
By refitting with a different reference level
The coefficient for studyarm1 is the arm effect in the reference level, so making the other level the reference gives its effect directly:


Click to show/hide R Code
participants_spanish_ref <- participants %>%
  mutate(prefer_language = relevel(prefer_language, ref = "Spanish"))

fit_spanish_ref <- glm.nb(
  rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(log(followup_time_itt)),
  data = participants_spanish_ref
)
# exp(coef(fit_spanish_ref)["studyarm1"]) is now the IRR in Spanish speakers


This is the same model, coded differently: it fits identically, and the interaction p-value doesn’t change. An earlier version of the plotting function used a related idea, rewriting the formula to expose subgroup-specific terms directly; the code now takes those effects from the fitted model with emmeans (see How this code does it).






NoteOptional: where the interval comes from





By hand from the coefficients
The arm effect in a non-reference level is a sum of coefficients, so its variance is a sum of variances and covariances. For the count model rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(...):
\[
\log \text{IRR}_{\text{Spanish}} = \beta_{\text{arm}} + \beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}}
\]
\[
\text{Var} = \text{Var}(\beta_{\text{arm}}) + \text{Var}(\beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}}) + 2\,\text{Cov}(\beta_{\text{arm}}, \beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}})
\]


Click to show/hide R Code
b <- coef(fit)
v <- vcov(fit)
terms <- c("studyarm1", "studyarm1:prefer_languageSpanish")

log_irr <- sum(b[terms])
se <- sqrt(sum(v[terms, terms]))     # the sum of the 2 x 2 block

exp(log_irr)                          # IRR in Spanish speakers
exp(log_irr + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se)


The same idea works for any combination: the arm difference at the 6-month visit in one subgroup level of a mixed model is the sum of the baseline arm term and the relevant two- and three-way terms.
Here coef() extracts coefficient estimates and vcov() extracts their variance–covariance matrix. The covariance matters because terms from the same model are estimated together. The square root of the combined variance gives a standard error. The displayed hand calculation uses a normal approximation; it is not a universal replacement for the degrees-of-freedom or interval method used by a mixed-model package.

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
Check that the methods agree
Equivalent contrasts from the same fitted model should agree when they use the same rows, coding, scale, degrees of freedom and interval method. Refitting can obscure those requirements, especially if missing predictors change the rows used. On synthetic data, compare the estimates and intervals explicitly before adopting a new reporting route. That validation is tracked in #9.

title: Interactions
text: This page explains what the coefficients of a model with an interaction mean, for the two kinds of model this analysis uses. It uses made-up numbers only.

title: Interactions
text:
Effect modification in a trial
A subgroup analysis asks whether the intervention’s effect differs between groups of participants: by preferred language, sex, child or adult, or baseline adherence or asthma control. The usual way to ask it is to add an arm × subgroup interaction to the model. The interaction lets the arm effect take a different value in each subgroup level.
An overall effect averages across the participants being compared. A subgroup analysis asks an additional question: does that effect differ by a characteristic such as preferred language? This does not mean language itself was randomized. The subgroup main effect should not be read as a causal effect of speaking one language rather than another.

title: Interactions
text:
Reading the coefficients: count models
For a count outcome with a two-level subgroup (say English and Spanish, with English as the reference level):


Click to show/hide R Code
glm.nb(
  rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(log(followup_time_itt)),
  data = participants
)


The model fits coefficients on a log scale. Applying exp() converts them to ratios. English is the reference level, the category used as the starting comparison; it is not a statement that English speakers are the typical or preferred population. After exponentiating:







Exponentiated coefficient
Meaning




studyarm1
Incidence rate ratio (IRR), intervention vs control, in the reference level only (English)


prefer_languageSpanish
Rate ratio, Spanish vs English, in the control arm only


studyarm1:prefer_languageSpanish
Ratio of the two IRRs: IRR in Spanish speakers ÷ IRR in English speakers



So a table of these terms never shows the arm effect in the second level directly. With made-up numbers: if studyarm1 is 0.80 and the interaction is 1.25, the IRR in English speakers is 0.80 and the IRR in Spanish speakers is 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00. The interaction of 1.25 isn’t an effect in anyone; it’s how much the effect changes between levels.

Keep three quantities separate
For the invented example above:








Quantity
Value
Interpretation




Intervention/control IRR in English speakers
0.80
Intervention rate is 20% lower


Intervention/control IRR in Spanish speakers
1.00
Equal modeled rates


Ratio of those IRRs
1.25
The arm comparison differs between subgroups



The last value is a comparison of comparisons. It does not mean Spanish speakers have 25% more events.

title: Interactions
section: Reading the coefficients: linear mixed models
text:
Reading the coefficients: linear mixed models
The same logic holds on an additive scale. In outcome ~ time_factor * studyarm * subgroup + (1 | id):

the two-way and three-way terms involving studyarm describe how the arm effect differs between visits and between subgroup levels;
each term is a difference: a difference between levels in the arm difference, or, for the three-way terms, a difference between levels in the change-from-baseline arm difference (see Longitudinal data and mixed models);
with six visits and a two-level subgroup there are 24 fixed effects, and the arm effect at a given visit in a given level is the sum of up to four of them.

In ordinary language, the three-way interaction asks: “Does the difference in improvement between the two arms also differ between subgroups?” Work out the arm comparison within each subgroup before comparing those comparisons.
That’s why tables of raw coefficients from these models are hard to read. What a p-value for interaction means explains what these terms’ p-values test, and Effects behind an interaction shows how to get the effects themselves.

title: Interactions
text:
Scale matters
An interaction is always measured on a scale. The count models are multiplicative (a ratio of IRRs); the mixed models are additive (a difference of differences). The same data can show an interaction on one scale and none on the other. For example, rates of 2 and 1 in one subgroup and 4 and 2 in another have the same ratio (2) in both, so no multiplicative interaction, but different differences (1 and 2), so an additive one. Knol and VanderWeele recommend reporting the effect within each stratum alongside interaction measures, so readers can judge both (Knol and VanderWeele 2012).
For a brief clinical-statistics explanation, read Altman and Bland on comparing two estimates (Altman and Bland 2003). For reporting guidance, Knol and VanderWeele explain why subgroup-specific effects belong alongside the interaction measure (Knol and VanderWeele 2012).

title: Overview
text:
This site explains the R analysis of the EM-ASTHMA pilot randomized trial, which compared the COHERO mobile app with control. Participants included adults and children with a caregiver. Assessments were scheduled at baseline and 2, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months. The analysis asks how outcomes differ between the assigned groups and whether those differences vary over time or between subgroups.
There are two main kinds of outcome. Questionnaire scores describe asthma control, quality of life, activity limitation and self-reported controller adherence at repeated visits. App medication records and health-care-use fields supply counts and measures of recorded use. Those different data structures need different statistical models.
The detailed intervention, eligibility criteria and choice of a primary outcome still need protocol information; the code alone cannot establish them. This site explains the implemented analysis and does not report trial findings.

title: How to read the trajectory figure
text:
Each repeated outcome in this analysis is shown in one kind of figure: the outcome at every visit, by arm, with the model’s estimates and the tests drawn from them. This page explains what each part of that figure shows and what it does not.
The two figures below are drawn from synthetic data, invented by the test code, so the numbers in them are not trial results. The subgroup in the second figure (“Example group”) is invented too.
crumbs: How to read the trajectory figure

title: How to read the trajectory figure
text:
One outcome, two arms



A synthetic example with the effect panel: model-estimated means by arm over the visits, the difference between arms below them, then p values and the number of participants observed at each visit.


Read the figure from top to bottom.
Points and bars. Each point is an arm’s mean at that visit, as estimated by the mixed model, and the bar is its 95% confidence interval. The interval describes how precisely the mean is estimated, not how spread out the participants are. The two arms are drawn slightly apart at each visit so their bars do not overlap; both belong to the same visit. Color, point shape and line type all differ between the arms, so the figure can be read in grayscale.
Faint lines (in the second figure) are each participant’s recorded values, joined across visits. They show the spread and the shape of individual courses that the means summarize. Some figures leave them out, and a figure for a group small enough to identify people should not be drawn this way at all.
The effect panel, when present, shows the comparison the trial is about: at each follow-up visit, the intervention arm’s change from baseline minus the control arm’s change from baseline, with its 95% confidence interval. Zero means no difference between the arms. This is not the same as the gap between the two plotted means at that visit, because it also takes away any difference between the arms at baseline.
p values are the tests of the same comparisons:

At baseline (month 0, no mark): whether the arms differ at the start.
At each follow-up (marked †): whether the arms differ in change from baseline, the difference shown in the effect panel.

They are shown to three decimals, and as “<0.001” when smaller. A blank means the model gave no estimate for that visit.
Observed, n is the number of participants in each arm with the outcome recorded at that visit. It falls when visits are missed. The means and intervals come from the model, which uses every recorded value, not only participants seen at every visit.
crumbs: How to read the trajectory figure

title: How to read the trajectory figure
text:
Figures by subgroup



A synthetic example by a three-level subgroup: one panel per level with individual trajectories and means, then p values within each level, the difference between levels, and the numbers observed.


When the analysis looks at a subgroup, each level gets its own panel with its own participants, all on the same scale. The p values under each panel test the intervention against the control within that level, read as above.
The row headed “difference between levels” asks a different question: is the effect in this level different from the effect in the first level? Each value sits under the level it concerns, and the first level, the reference, has none. This compares one level with the reference; it is not a single test of whether the effect differs across all the levels. What a p-value for interaction means explains why these tests answer a different question from the within-level ones, and why they need more data to detect a difference.
When three or more levels share the width, alternate p values sit on a second line so that they do not run into each other. They still line up with their visits.
crumbs: How to read the trajectory figure

title: How to read the trajectory figure
text:
Cautions

Many tests, no adjustment. Each figure carries a p value for every visit, and the analysis has many figures. None of the p values is adjusted for multiple comparisons, so some small p values are expected by chance.
Intervals that overlap can still belong to arms that differ, and intervals that do not overlap are not a test. Use the effect panel or the p value for the comparison.
The same figure, read differently. The same picture of means can come from different patterns in individuals. The faint lines, where shown, are the check.

How this code does it says which code produces each element.

title: How this code does it
text:
This page maps the ideas on the other methods pages to the analysis code, as it stands now, and notes what is planned to change.
Think of the workflow in three steps: prepare the observations, fit the model, then turn the fit into a table or plot. An R object can hold any of these, so its name alone does not tell you whether it contains data, a fitted model or formatted output.

title: How this code does it
text:
Fitting and tables
fit_mixed_model() fits outcome ~ time_factor * studyarm + (1 | study_id_screening), or the three-way version with a subgroup. 5. Fit mixed models fits each of the 56 analyses once: 5 outcomes overall, 5 outcomes × 4 subgroups, and 3 outcomes by child or adult, each in the intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations. Each fitted model then goes to the table, the estimates and, through the estimates, the plot.
tabulate_model_terms() shows the raw coefficients described on Longitudinal data and mixed models and Interactions: the baseline arm difference, the change-from-baseline differences at each visit, and the interaction terms. It doesn’t show the arm effect in each subgroup level directly.

title: How this code does it
text:
Estimates and plots
estimate_effects() takes everything the plot shows from that one fitted model, with emmeans (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026):







Estimate
What it’s used for




Mean in each visit × arm cell (and subgroup level), with its 95% confidence interval
The points and bars on the plot


Arm difference at baseline, and the visit × arm interaction at each follow-up (marked †), within each subgroup level
The p-values printed above each visit, or in each level’s panel


Difference in that effect between each subgroup level and the first level
The row of p-values under each level after the first



Degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite’s, the same method as the model table, and p-values are not adjusted for multiplicity. An earlier version of the code refitted the same model in up to three other codings to read these numbers off as coefficients; emmeans gives the same numbers from the one fit (checked on synthetic data, #10). Using one fit also means the means, the p-values and the table come from the same analysis rows.
compose_trajectory_figure() draws those estimates, optionally over the individual trajectories. It fits nothing. By default it shows the means and the p-values for the contrasts; with show_effect_panel = TRUE it also shows each contrast’s estimate and 95% confidence interval. At follow-up, the dagger-marked p-values concern change from baseline, not just the gap between the plotted means.
To read a plot, first identify the outcome, population, visit and subgroup. Then distinguish the individual observations, the fitted mean and its interval, and the particular contrast tested by each p-value. A visually separated pair of mean intervals is not a substitute for the corresponding contrast calculation.

title: How this code does it
text:
Count models
4. Fit count models fits negative binomial models with log follow-up time as the offset, overall and with each arm × subgroup interaction, and reports exponentiated coefficients: IRRs, and for the interaction terms, ratios of IRRs. As with the mixed-model tables, the IRR in the non-reference level of a subgroup isn’t shown directly. The separate alternative rescue fits retain an offset-syntax defect documented on the count-model page.

title: How this code does it
text:
What is planned to change
These are implementation proposals, not prerequisites for understanding the current analysis. Changing formatting and extracting a contrast can leave a model unchanged; changing the sample or formula can change the scientific comparison.

#8: move all tables to gtsummary. The decision to report both kinds of table, the model terms and the effects within each subgroup level, is recorded there.
#25: run the examples on these Methods pages on synthetic data, where the true effects are known.

Table 1

title: Functions
text:
Reusable helper functions. Each takes its inputs as arguments.
Each repeated-outcome analysis runs in three steps: fit the model once, estimate effects from it, then report them as a table and a plot. The names are general (an exposure, a time variable and an optional modifier), so the same functions serve any exposure-by-time analysis, with or without a subgroup.

title: Functions
text:
Fit mixed model
fit_mixed_model() accepts a visit dataset, the outcome column’s name and an optional modifier (subgroup) name. Without a modifier it fits visit × arm with a random intercept for each participant; with one, visit × arm × modifier. It returns the fitted model, which the next three functions all use.
What the model’s coefficients mean is explained in Longitudinal data and mixed models and Interactions.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Linear mixed model of an outcome on time (as a factor) by exposure, with a
# random intercept for each participant. With a modifier, the model is time
# by exposure by modifier.
fit_mixed_model <- function(data, outcome, modifier = NULL,
                            exposure = "studyarm", time = "time_factor",
                            id = "study_id_screening") {
  fixed_effects <- paste(c(time, exposure, modifier), collapse = " * ")
  model_formula <- paste0(
    outcome, " ~ ", fixed_effects, " + (1 | ", id, ")"
  ) %>%
    as.formula()

  lmer(model_formula, data = data)
}

title: Functions
text:
Tabulate model terms
tabulate_model_terms() turns a fitted model into a table of its coefficients. tidy() makes the model output table-shaped, and flextable() formats it. How this code does it describes what this table shows and doesn’t.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The fitted model's coefficients as a flextable: the baseline exposure
# difference, the time-by-exposure interaction terms and, with a modifier,
# the three-way terms
tabulate_model_terms <- function(fit, caption) {
  fit %>%
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    flextable() %>%
    set_caption(caption)
}

title: Functions
text:
Estimate effects
estimate_effects() asks emmeans for the numbers the plot needs, from the fitted model and without refitting: the mean in each visit × arm cell (and subgroup level), the arm effect at each visit within each level, and, with a subgroup, how that effect differs between levels. It returns them as tidy tables. Effects behind an interaction explains the method.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Estimates from a fitted model, with emmeans: the mean in each time x
# exposure (x modifier level) cell, and for each modifier level the exposure
# effect at each time. At the first (baseline) time the effect is the
# exposure difference; at later times it is the time-by-exposure interaction,
# the change from baseline in the exposed group minus that in the reference
# group. With a modifier, the difference in that effect between each level
# and the first level. Degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite's, as in the
# model table, and p values are not adjusted for multiplicity.
estimate_effects <- function(fit, exposure = "studyarm",
                             time = "time_factor", modifier = NULL) {
  emm <- function(specs, by = NULL) {
    emmeans(fit, specs = specs, by = by,
            lmer.df = "satterthwaite", lmerTest.limit = Inf)
  }
  tidy_emm <- function(x) {
    as_tibble(as.data.frame(summary(x, infer = TRUE, adjust = "none")))
  }
  first <- "trt.vs.ctrl1"
  baseline <- ref_grid(fit)@levels[[time]][1]
  # The later time in a "t - baseline" interaction contrast
  contrast_time <- function(x) str_remove(x, " - .*$")

  means <- emm(exposure, by = c(time, modifier)) %>%
    tidy_emm() %>%
    rename(estimate = emmean, conf.low = lower.CL, conf.high = upper.CL)

  at_baseline <- emm(exposure, by = c(time, modifier)) %>%
    contrast(first) %>%
    tidy_emm() %>%
    filter(.data[[time]] == baseline)
  over_time <- emm(c(exposure, time), by = modifier) %>%
    contrast(interaction = c(first, first)) %>%
    tidy_emm() %>%
    mutate(!!time := contrast_time(.data[[paste0(time, "_", first)]]))
  within_levels <- bind_rows(at_baseline, over_time) %>%
    select(any_of(c(modifier, time)), estimate, conf.low = lower.CL,
           conf.high = upper.CL, p.value)

  between_levels <- NULL
  if (!is.null(modifier)) {
    between_at_baseline <- emm(c(exposure, modifier), by = time) %>%
      contrast(interaction = c(first, first)) %>%
      tidy_emm() %>%
      filter(.data[[time]] == baseline)
    between_over_time <- emm(c(exposure, time, modifier)) %>%
      contrast(interaction = c(first, first, first)) %>%
      tidy_emm() %>%
      mutate(!!time := contrast_time(.data[[paste0(time, "_", first)]]))
    between_levels <- bind_rows(between_at_baseline, between_over_time) %>%
      mutate(
        comparison = .data[[paste0(modifier, "_", first)]],
        .before = 1
      ) %>%
      select(comparison, all_of(time), estimate, conf.low = lower.CL,
             conf.high = upper.CL, p.value)
  }

  list(
    means = means %>%
      select(
        all_of(c(time, exposure, modifier)), estimate, conf.low, conf.high
      ),
    within_levels = within_levels,
    between_levels = between_levels
  )
}

title: Functions
Plot style
text: The house style for figures: one theme with its colours, shapes and line types, readable labels, and one way to save a figure at its printed size.

title: Plot style
Plot style
text:
Palettes
A palette is the ordered set of colours (or shapes, or line types) given to the groups in a figure. The colours are the Okabe-Ito set, chosen to stay distinguishable for people with the common kinds of colour-vision deficiency, with a neutral dark grey first so the control arm recedes and the intervention arm stands out. Groups also differ by point shape and line type, so a figure still works in greyscale and never relies on colour alone.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Okabe-Ito colours (safe for the common kinds of colour-vision deficiency),
# with a neutral dark grey first: the first group of any factor, such as the
# control arm or a reference level, is drawn in grey and the second in blue
okabe_ito <- unname(grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito"))
publication_colours <- c("#555555", okabe_ito[c(6, 7, 4, 2, 8, 3, 5)])

# Shapes and line types differ too, so groups never rely on colour alone.
# Filled shapes 21-25 take a white fill, so overlapping points stay visible.
publication_shapes <- c(21, 24, 22, 23, 25)
publication_linetypes <- c("22", "solid", "42", "12", "4212")

title: Plot style
text:
The publication theme
A theme controls everything in a figure that is not data: background, gridlines, text sizes, legend position. theme_publication() keeps only what helps a reader: light horizontal gridlines to read values against, thin axis lines, no panel border. It also carries the palettes above, so a figure needs no colour settings of its own. Text sizes are set for the printed figure (9 points by default), so a figure should be saved at the size it will be printed.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A quiet theme for print: no panel border, light horizontal gridlines only,
# thin axis lines, text sized for the printed figure. The legend sits above
# the panel; figures that name their groups on the plot itself remove it.
theme_publication <- function(base_size = 9, base_family = "",
                              header_family = NULL) {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(
    base_size = base_size,
    base_family = base_family,
    header_family = header_family
  ) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(
        colour = "grey90", linewidth = 0.3
      ),
      axis.line.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.ticks.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "grey20"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "grey30"),
      strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "grey35", hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left",
      palette.colour.discrete = publication_colours,
      palette.fill.discrete = publication_colours,
      palette.shape.discrete = scales::pal_manual(publication_shapes),
      palette.linetype.discrete = publication_linetypes
    )
}

title: Plot style
Plot style
text:
Saving a figure
save_figure() writes a figure at its printed size in millimetres, in each format needed: PDF and SVG, which keep lines and text sharp at any zoom, for journals; and PNG for the website. The PDF device embeds fonts and handles symbols such as the dagger (†). Nothing in the analysis saves a figure yet; this is the function to use when it does.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Save a figure at its printed size, in millimetres: PDF (cairo, which embeds
# fonts and handles symbols such as the dagger) and SVG for journals, PNG
# (ragg) for the website. Returns the paths written.
save_figure <- function(plot, file, width, height,
                        formats = c("pdf", "svg", "png"), dpi = 600) {
  devices <- list(
    pdf = grDevices::cairo_pdf,
    svg = svglite::svglite,
    png = ragg::agg_png
  )
  paths <- paste0(file, ".", formats)
  for (i in seq_along(formats)) {
    ggplot2::ggsave(
      paths[i], plot,
      device = devices[[formats[i]]],
      width = width, height = height, units = "mm", dpi = dpi,
      bg = "white"
    )
  }
  invisible(paths)
}

title: Plot style
text:
The default theme
Setting the theme once makes it the starting point for every figure, including quick ones made while exploring. The figures in Figures also add it themselves, so each figure looks the same however it is printed, including in the snapshot tests.


Click to show/hide R Code

ggplot2::set_theme(theme_publication())


For more on themes and on choosing colours, see Fundamentals of Data Visualization by Claus Wilke.

title: 2. Build visit data
text: Build the visit-level analysis data for the ITT and per-protocol populations, with recodes and scale scores.

title: 2. Build visit data
text:
Build visit data
The input is the imported REDCap table; the intended output still has one row per participant and recorded visit. mutate() creates or changes columns without summarizing the rows. case_when() maps each event name to its scheduled month. time_linear stores that number; time_factor stores the visit as a category for the models.
The code groups by participant before fill() carries baseline information down later rows. This assumes the baseline row precedes the rows that need it. It carries assignment and baseline subgroup information, not a missed visit’s outcome score. See the fill documentation for direction and grouping (tidyr authors, n.d.).
Selected 999 codes become NA, R’s missing-value marker. The separate language recode currently assigns 999 to English; that behavior is under review in #16. Scores are then derived from the item columns: rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE) averages available items within a row. It does not establish that an instrument permits a score with that many unanswered items; scoring rules remain to be verified against the instruments.
The baseline adherence and asthma-control groups are carried to later visits, so a participant does not switch subgroup because a later score changes. The small horizontal time shift is only for separating points in plots. For the R verbs in this block, see Data transformation (Wickham et al. 2023).


Click to show/hide R Code
clean_asthma_data_itt <- clean_asthma_data %>%
  # Months since baseline for each REDCap event
  mutate(time_linear = case_when(
    redcap_event_name == "baseline_arm_1" ~ 0,
    redcap_event_name == "2month_followup_arm_1" ~ 2,
    redcap_event_name == "4month_followup_arm_1" ~ 4,
    redcap_event_name == "6month_followup_arm_1" ~ 6,
    redcap_event_name == "9month_followup_arm_1" ~ 9,
    redcap_event_name == "12month_followup_arm_1" ~ 12
  )) %>%
  # A preferred language of 999 is set to English. See issue #16.
  mutate(prefer_language = ifelse(
    prefer_language == 999,
    1,
    prefer_language
  )) %>%
  # Visit time as a factor, for models that treat time as categorical
  mutate(time_factor = as_factor(time_linear)) %>%
  mutate(studyarm = as.factor(studyarm)) %>%
  mutate(participant_sex = factor(
    participant_sex,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("Male", "Female")
  )) %>%
  mutate(child_adult = factor(
    child_adult,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("Child", "Adult")
  )) %>%
  mutate(prefer_language = factor(
    prefer_language,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("English", "Spanish")
  )) %>%
  # These are recorded only at baseline; carry them to every visit
  group_by(study_id_screening) %>%
  fill(
    studyarm, child_adult, prefer_language, consent_date,
    follow_up_2_months, follow_up_4_months, follow_up_6_months,
    follow_up_9_months, follow_up_12_month
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(across(
    all_of(c(aqlq_items, pacqlq_items, afs_items, missing_999_variables)),
    ~ ifelse(.x == 999, NA, .x)
  )) %>%
  # Date of each visit, from the consent and follow-up dates
  mutate(date_of_observation = case_when(
    redcap_event_name == "baseline_arm_1" ~ consent_date,
    redcap_event_name == "2month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_2_months,
    redcap_event_name == "4month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_4_months,
    redcap_event_name == "6month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_6_months,
    redcap_event_name == "9month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_9_months,
    redcap_event_name == "12month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_12_month
  )) %>%
  # Visits after the app update glitch
  mutate(post_glitch_date = (date_of_observation > glitch_date)) %>%
  # Self-reported controller adherence score. See analysis-plan.md.
  mutate(self_reported_adherence = 32 -
    only_give_controller_medication_needed -
    only_give_controller_medication_breathless +
    give_controller_medication_regularly -
    try_to_avoid_controller_medication -
    forget_give_controller_medication -
    alter_change_dosage_controller_medication -
    stop_giving_controller_medication -
    reserve_controller_medication_if_treatment_not_work -
    give_controller_medication_child_does_breathless +
    give_controller_medication_as_label) %>%
  # Baseline adherence and asthma control groups, carried to every visit
  mutate(self_reported_adherence_binary = case_when(
    self_reported_adherence >= adherence_cutoff &
      time_factor == "0" ~ "Adherent",
    self_reported_adherence < adherence_cutoff &
      time_factor == "0" ~ "Non-adherent"
  )) %>%
  mutate(
    self_reported_adherence_binary = as.factor(self_reported_adherence_binary)
  ) %>%
  mutate(act_binary = case_when(
    act_score >= act_cutoff & time_factor == "0" ~ "Controlled",
    act_score < act_cutoff & time_factor == "0" ~ "Uncontrolled"
  )) %>%
  mutate(act_binary = as.factor(act_binary)) %>%
  group_by(study_id_screening) %>%
  fill(self_reported_adherence_binary, act_binary) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Each score is the mean of the items answered at that visit
  mutate(aqlq_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(aqlq_items)), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    pacqlq_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(pacqlq_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(afs_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(afs_items)), na.rm = TRUE))

title: 2. Build visit data
text:
Per protocol population
clean_asthma_data_itt retains the visit records for the intention-to-treat analysis, which compares participants by assigned arm. The project’s per-protocol dataset is a filtered copy keeping observations on or before the app-glitch cutoff. Here, “per protocol” means this specific date restriction, not a general selection of participants who adhered to treatment. A missing visit date produces a missing comparison and is not retained by filter(post_glitch_date == FALSE). The two datasets feed the same model code later.


Click to show/hide R Code
clean_asthma_data_pp <- clean_asthma_data_itt %>%
  filter(post_glitch_date == FALSE)

title: 2. Build visit data
text:
Study dates
Filtering to baseline makes a participant-level lookup table of consent and scheduled follow-up dates. The medication script joins this lookup onto app records to place them within each participant’s follow-up. Check that the lookup has one row per participant: otherwise each medication record could match several rows. A blank follow-up date also needs attention because later comparisons against that date cannot establish whether a record is in the window.

study_dates <- clean_asthma_data_itt %>%
  filter(time_linear == 0) %>%
  select(
    study_id_screening, consent_date, follow_up_2_months,
    follow_up_4_months, follow_up_6_months, follow_up_9_months,
    follow_up_12_month
  )

text: Attach packages and define constants shared by every script.

title: Setup
text:
Load packages
A few R symbols recur throughout the site: <- stores a result under a name; %>% passes the result on the left into the next operation; $ selects a named column; and [["name"]] selects an item from a named list. Read a pipeline from top to bottom, asking how each step changes the rows or columns.
A package supplies functions that R does not provide on its own. library() attaches an already installed package for this session; it does not install it. Here, readxl reads spreadsheets, dplyr/tidyr (within tidyverse) reshape data, MASS and lme4 fit models, and the table and plotting packages format the output. If R reports that a package is missing, the setup has not finished.

library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(ggbeeswarm)

title: Setup
text:
Data paths
COHERO_DATA_DIR is a setting supplied by an authorized analyst outside the repository. Sys.getenv() reads that setting and file.path() combines it with each filename. The explicit stop() prevents the script from continuing with an unspecified data folder. Reading this website does not require the files: its code blocks are displayed, not executed.

}

redcap_export_file <- file.path(

title: 1. Import data
text:
Import REDCap
The REDCap export supplies participant-visit records. Sex comes from a separate participant file. A left_join() matches the participant identifier and adds sex to each matching visit, retaining rows from the visit file. Repeated visits for one participant are expected; repeated matches in the sex file could instead multiply rows unintentionally. An authorized analyst should check that the sex file has one row per identifier and that the join preserves the visit count.
The illustrated joins in R for Data Science explain keys and unmatched rows (Wickham et al. 2023). The output here, clean_asthma_data, becomes the input to Build visit data.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Raw data export from REDCap
raw_asthma_data <- read_excel(redcap_export_file)

# Sex is in a separate file
baseline_sex <- read_excel(baseline_sex_file) %>%
  select(study_id_screening, participant_sex)

# Merge sex into the REDCap export
clean_asthma_data <- left_join(
  raw_asthma_data,
  baseline_sex,
  by = "study_id_screening"
)

title: 1. Import data
text:
Import notifications
This reads the Notifications sheet into raw_notifications. col_types states how successive spreadsheet columns should be interpreted: numeric, text or date; skip omits a column. Removing spaces standardizes the column names used in R. These notification records are imported but are not an outcome in the model scripts shown on this site.


Click to show/hide R Code
raw_notifications <- read_excel(
  push_data_file,
  sheet = "Notifications",
  col_types = c(
    "numeric", "numeric", "text", "date", "skip",
    "numeric", "text", "date", "skip", "skip"
  )
)

# Remove spaces from names
names(raw_notifications) <- names(raw_notifications) %>%
  str_replace_all(fixed(" "), "")

title: 1. Import data
text:
Import medications
This reads individual app medication records into raw_medications; a participant can contribute many rows. This is a different unit of observation from a visit or a participant. Derive medication outcomes will aggregate these records. The current import suppresses warnings, so absence of a displayed warning does not verify that every cell was parsed correctly. readxl’s column-type guide explains what happens when spreadsheet cells and requested types disagree (readxl authors, n.d.).


Click to show/hide R Code
# suppressWarnings avoids one warning per missing cell
raw_medications <- read_excel(
  push_data_file,
  sheet = "Medication Usage",
  col_types = c(
    "numeric", "date", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "text", "date",
    "numeric", "text", "text", "text", "text", "text", "text", "text",
    "numeric", "numeric", "date", "date", "date", "date", "date"
  )
) %>%
  suppressWarnings()

# Remove spaces from names
names(raw_medications) <- names(raw_medications) %>%
  str_replace_all(fixed(" "), "")

title: 1. Import data
text:
Import followup dates
This loads the separate timepoint-review spreadsheet as raw_followup_dates and simplifies its column names. Loading a file does not mean later scripts use it: the study_dates object used for medication windows is built from the baseline REDCap rows in the next script. Keeping track of which object supplies a date is essential when checking follow-up windows.


Click to show/hide R Code
# suppressWarnings avoids one warning per missing cell
raw_followup_dates <- read_excel(
  timepoint_review_file,
  col_types = c("numeric", "date", "date", "date", "date", "date", "date")
) %>%
  suppressWarnings()

# Remove spaces and other troublesome characters from names
names(raw_followup_dates) <- names(raw_followup_dates) %>%
  str_replace_all(fixed(" "), "") %>%
  str_replace_all(fixed("#"), "") %>%
  str_replace_all(fixed("-"), "")
